source_text: Καὶ περὶ μὲν τοῦ παρ’ Ἑβραίων τὰ τῶν φιλοσόφων ἐσκευωρῆσθαι δόγματα μικρὸν ὕστερον διαληψόμεθα, πρότερον δέ, ὅπερ ἀκόλουθον ἦν, περὶ τῶν κατὰ Μωυσέα χρόνων ἤδη λεκτέον, δἰ ὧν δειχθήσεται ἀναμφηρίστως πάσης σοφίας ἀρχαιοτάτη ἡ κατὰ Ἑβραίους φιλοσοφία. εἴρηται μὲν οὖν περὶ τούτων ἀκριβῶς Τατιανῷ ἐν τῷ Πρὸς Ἕλληνας, εἴρηται δὲ καὶ Κασσιανῷ ἐν τῷ πρώτῳ τῶν Ἐξηγητικῶν· ἀπαιτεῖ δὲ ὅμως τὸ ὑπόμνημα καὶ ἡμᾶς ἐπιδραμεῖν τὰ κατὰ τὸν τόπον εἰρημένα. Ἀπίων τοίνυν ὁ γραμματικός, ὁ Πλειστονίκης ἐπικληθείς, ἐν τῇ τετάρτῃ τῶν Αἰγυπτιακῶν ἱστοριῶν, καίτοι φιλαπεχθημόνως πρὸς Ἑβραίους διακείμενος, ἅτε Αἰγύπτιος τὸ γένος, ὡς καὶ κατὰ Ἰουδαίων συντάξασθαι βιβλίον, Ἀμώσιος τοῦ Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέως μεμνημένος καὶ τῶν κατ’ αὐτὸν πράξεων, μάρτυρα παρατίθεται Πτολεμαῖον τὸν Μενδήσιον. καὶ τὰ τῆς λέξεως αὐτοῦ ὧδε ἔχει· κατέσκαψε δὲ τὴν Ἀουαρίαν Ἄμωσις κατὰ τὸν Ἀργεῖον γενόμενος Ἴναχον, ὡς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις ἀνέγραφεν ὁ Μενδήσιος Πτολεμαῖος. ὁ δὲ Πτολεμαῖος οὗτος ἱερεὺς μὲν ἦν, τὰς δὲ τῶν Αἰγυπτίων βασιλέων πράξεις ἐν τρισὶν ὅλαις ἐκθέμενος βίβλοις κατὰ Ἄμωσίν φησιν Αἰγύπτου βασιλέα Μωυσέως ἡγουμένου γεγονέναι Ἰουδαίοις τὴν ἐξ Αἰγύπτου πορείαν, ἐξ ὧν συνῶπται κατὰ Ἴναχον ἠκμακέναι τὸν Μωσέα. παλαίτατα δὲ τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν τὰ Ἀργολικά, τὰ ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου λέγω, ὡς Διονύσιος ὁ Ἁλικαρνασσεὺς ἐν τοῖς Χρόνοις διδάσκει, τούτων δὲ † τεσσαράκοντα μὲν γενεαῖς νεώτερα τὰ Ἀττικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Κέκροπος τοῦ διφυοῦς δὴ καὶ αὐτόχθονος, ὥς φησι κατὰ λέξιν ὁ Τατιανός, ἐννέα δὲ τὰ Ἀρκαδικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Πελασγοῦ· λέγεται δὲ καὶ οὗτος αὐτόχθων. τούτων δὲ ἄλλαιν δυοῖν νεώτερα τὰ Φθιωτικὰ τὰ ἀπὸ Δευκαλίωνος. εἰς δὲ τὸν χρόνον τῶν Τρωϊκῶν ἀπὸ Ἰνάχου γενεαὶ μὲν εἴκοσι ἢ μιᾷ πλείους διαριθμοῦνται, ἔτη δέ, ὡς ἔπος εἰπεῖν, τετρακόσια καὶ πρόσω. εἰ δὲ τὰ Ἀσσυρίων πολλοῖς ἔτεσι πρεσβύτερα τῶν Ἑλληνικῶν ἀφ’ ὧν Κτησίας λέγει, φανήσεται τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τετρακοσιοστῷ ἔτει τῆς Ἀσσυρίων ἀρχῆς, τῆς δὲ Βηλούχου τοῦ ὀγδόου δυναστείας τῷ δευτέρῳ καὶ τριακοστῷ ἡ Μωυσέως κατὰ Ἄμωσιν τὸν Αἰγύπτιον καὶ κατὰ Ἴναχον τὸν Ἀργεῖον ἐξ Αἰγύπτου κίνησις. ἦν δὲ κατὰ τὴν Ἑλλάδα κατὰ μὲν Φορωνέα τὸν μετὰ Ἴναχον ὁ ἐπὶ Ὠγύγου κατακλυσμὸς καὶ ἡ ἐν Σικυῶνι βασιλεία, πρώτου μὲν Αἰγιαλέως, εἶτα Εὔρωπος, εἶτα Τελχῖνος, καὶ ἡ Κρητὸς ἐν Κρήτῃ. Ἀκουσίλαος γὰρ Φορωνέα πρῶτον ἄνθρωπον γενέσθαι λέγει· ὅθεν καὶ ὁ τῆς Φορωνίδος ποιητὴς εἶναι αὐτὸν ἔφη πατέρα θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων. ἐντεῦθεν ὁ Πλάτων ἐν Τιμαίῳ κατακολουθήσας Ἀκουσιλάῳ γράφει· καί ποτε προαγαγεῖν βουληθεὶς αὐτοὺς περὶ τῶν ἀρχαίων εἰς λόγους τῶν τῇδε τῇ πόλει τὰ ἀρχαιότατα λέγειν ἐπιχειρεῖ, περὶ Φορωνέως τε τοῦ πρώτου λεχθέντος καὶ Νιόβης, καὶ τὰ μετὰ τὸν κατακλυσμόν. κατὰ δὲ Φόρβαντα Ἀκταῖος, ἀφ’ οὗ Ἀκταία ἡ Ἀττική. κατὰ δὲ Τριόπαν Προμηθεὺς καὶ Ἄτλας καὶ Ἐπιμηθεὺς καὶ ὁ διφυὴς Κέκροψ καὶ Ἰώ. κατὰ δὲ Κρότωπον ἡ ἐπὶ Φαέθοντος ἐκπύρωσις καὶ ἡ ἐπὶ Δευκαλίωνος ἐπομβρία. κατὰ δὲ Σθένελον ἥ τε Ἀμφικτυόνος βασιλεία καὶ ἡ εἰς Πελοπόννησον Δαναοῦ παρουσία καὶ ἡ ὑπὸ Δαρδάνου τῆς Δαρδανίας κτίσις, ὃν πρῶτον, φησὶν Ὅμηρος, τέκετο νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς, ἥ τε τῆς Εὐρώπης εἰς Κρήτην ἐκ Φοινίκης ἀνακομιδή.
pass_a_gloss: And a little later we will discuss how the doctrines of the philosophers were seen among the Hebrews, but first, as was fitting, we must speak about the times of Moses, through which it will be shown clearly that the Hebrew philosophy is the most ancient of all wisdom. Now, Tatian has spoken precisely about these things in his work Against the Greeks, and also Cassian has spoken in the first of his Exegetical works; however, the memorandum also demands that we run through the things said according to the place. Apion the grammarian, also called Plistonicus, in the fourth book of his Egyptian histories, although he is hostile towards the Hebrews, being an Egyptian by birth, and has even written a book against the Jews, mentions Amosis, king of the Egyptians, and the events that occurred during his reign, and presents Ptolemy of Mendes as a witness. And the words of the latter are as follows: Amosis, having become king in the place of Argive Inachus, dug up the city of Avaris, as Ptolemy of Mendes wrote in his Chronicles. Now, this Ptolemy was a priest, and in three books he set forth the deeds of the Egyptian kings, and he says that during the reign of Amosis, king of Egypt, the Jews, led by Moses, made their journey out of Egypt, from which it is clear that Moses flourished during the time of Inachus. But the most ancient of the Greek things are the Argolic, which I call the things from Inachus, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his Chronicles. And the Attic things, which are from Cecrops, the two-natured and autochthonous, as Tatian says word for word, are forty generations younger than these, and the Arcadic things, which are from Pelasgus, are nine generations younger; and this Pelasgus is also said to be autochthonous. And the Phthiotic things, which are from Deucalion, are younger than these by two generations. Now, from Inachus to the time of the Trojan War, twenty or a few more generations are counted, and years, so to speak, about four hundred. But if the Assyrian things are much older than the Greek things, as Ctesias says, it will be clear that in the second and four hundredth year of the Assyrian reign, and in the second and thirtieth year of the eighth dynasty of Belochus, the movement of Moses out of Egypt, during the reign of Amosis the Egyptian and Inachus the Argive, took place. Now, in Greece, during the time of Phoroneus, who came after Inachus, there was the flood in the time of Ogygus and the kingdom in Sicyon, first of Aegialeus, then of Eurypus, then of Telchin, and the kingdom of Crete in Crete. For Acusilaus says that Phoroneus was the first man to be born; hence the poet of the Phoroneis says that he was the father of mortal men. From this, Plato, following Acusilaus, writes in the Timaeus: and at one time, wishing to lead them on to discussions about the ancient things of this city, he attempts to speak about the most ancient things, about Phoroneus, who was said to be the first, and about Niobe, and about the things after the flood. According to Phorbas, there was Actaeus, from whom the Attic Actaea comes. According to Triopas, there were Prometheus and Atlas and Epimetheus and the two-natured Cecrops and Io. According to Crotopus, there was the conflagration in the time of Phaethon and the flood in the time of Deucalion. According to Sthenelus, there was the kingdom of Amphictyon and the arrival of Danaus in Peloponnese and the foundation of Dardania by Dardanus, whom Homer says was the firstborn of cloud-gathering Zeus, and the migration of Europe from Phoenicia to Crete.
pass_b_english: We shall shortly examine how the doctrines of the philosophers were seen among the Hebrews; first, however, as is fitting, we must speak of the times of Moses, through which it will be shown beyond dispute that the Hebrew philosophy is the most ancient of all wisdom. Tatian has already treated these matters precisely in his *Address to the Greeks*, and Cassian has done so in the first book of his *Exegetical Works*; nevertheless, the present memorandum also requires us to run through what has been said on the topic.

Apion the grammarian, surnamed Plistonicus, in the fourth book of his *Egyptian Histories* — although he is hostile toward the Hebrews, being Egyptian by birth, and has even composed a work against the Jews — mentions Amosis, king of the Egyptians, and the events of his reign, and cites Ptolemy of Mendes as a witness. Ptolemy's words run thus: Amosis, having become king in the time of Argive Inachus, demolished the city of Avaris, as Ptolemy of Mendes recorded in his *Chronicles*. This Ptolemy was a priest, and in three books he set forth the deeds of the Egyptian kings; he states that during the reign of Amosis, king of Egypt, the Jews, led by Moses, made their journey out of Egypt, from which it follows that Moses flourished in the time of Inachus.

The most ancient of Greek history is the Argolic — that is, the history reckoned from Inachus — as Dionysius of Halicarnassus teaches in his *Chronicles*. The Attic history, reckoned from Cecrops the two-natured and autochthonous, is, as Tatian says word for word, forty generations younger; the Arcadian history, reckoned from Pelasgus, is nine generations younger, and Pelasgus too is said to be autochthonous. The Phthiotic history, reckoned from Deucalion, is younger still by two generations. From Inachus to the time of the Trojan War, twenty or a few more generations are counted, amounting, so to speak, to about four hundred years.

If the Assyrian history is far older than the Greek, as Ctesias says, it will appear that in the four hundred and second year of the Assyrian empire, and in the thirty-second year of the eighth dynasty of Belochus, the migration of Moses out of Egypt took place under Amosis the Egyptian and Inachus the Argive. In Greece, during the time of Phoroneus, who came after Inachus, there occurred the flood of Ogygus and the kingdom in Sicyon — first of Aegialeus, then of Eurypus, then of Telchin — and the kingdom of Crete in Crete. Acusilaus declares that Phoroneus was the first man born; hence the poet of the *Phoroneis* calls him the father of mortal men. Following Acusilaus, Plato writes in the *Timaeus* that, wishing to draw his interlocutors into discourse about ancient things, he undertakes to speak of the most ancient traditions of the city: of Phoroneus, said to be the first, of Niobe, and of the events after the flood.

Under Phorbas came Actaeus, from whom the Attic Actaea takes its name. Under Triopas came Prometheus, Atlas, Epimetheus, the two-natured Cecrops, and Io. Under Crotopus occurred the conflagration in the time of Phaethon and the flood in the time of Deucalion. Under Sthenelus came the kingdom of Amphictyon, the arrival of Danaus in the Peloponnese, and the foundation of Dardania by Dardanus, whom Homer says was the firstborn of cloud-gathering Zeus, together with the carrying off of Europa from Phoenicia to Crete.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex chronological arguments and the list of mythological figures. Pass A preserves the clause structure and nuances of the Greek, while Pass B provides a fluent rendering that adheres to the source. All scripture/author citations (Tatian, Cassian, Apion, Ptolemy, Dionysius, Ctesias, Acusilaus, Plato, Homer) are correctly handled and matched to the text.
